Lesson 01

Write a one-page safety policy

Why it matters

Name the data, the tools, the actions that need a person, and what you will not build.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
01 of 05
Time
11 min
Level
Core
Length
One page
Names
Data, tools, human actions
Includes
What you will not build

A policy you can apply is one page. A policy that quotes every guideline and changes nothing is not a control.

Data I will send to a hosted model:
Data that stays on this machine:
Tools the system may call unattended:
Actions that always wait for a person:
What I will not build:
Where traces live and when I delete them:

Fill it for the capstone before you connect a tool. If a line is 'not sure', the tool stays disconnected. Update the page when the system changes, in the same change as the tool list.

Practice

Fill the six lines. Use 'none yet' where that is true.

Check

What do you do with a tool that is not on the policy page?

Show the answer

You do not enable it. The page is the allowlist.

Lesson 02

Decide retention before you log the prompt

Why it matters

Prompts are often personal data. A debug log is a database.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
02 of 05
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Prompts
Often personal data
A log
A database
Needs
An end date

A prompt can contain a person's name, a health note, a customer message, or a secret. The provider's retention setting and your own log are two different stores. Configure both. 'The vendor probably deletes it' is not a setting.

  • Prefer not to send private data. Retrieve or redact locally first when you can.
  • Set the provider retention and training-opt-out flags you actually need. Re-read them when you change accounts.
  • Give your logs a lifetime. A disk that keeps every prompt forever will surprise you in an incident.
  • Deletion is a feature: how a person asks, and how you prove the trace is gone.

Synthetic fixtures belong in the repo. Real prompts do not, unless the repo is private and approved for that data. This course's exercises use synthetic fixtures for that reason.

Practice

Add two lines to your policy page: how long traces live, and what you will redact before a trace is written.

Check

Name two stores that can retain a prompt.

Show the answer

The provider, according to the settings on that key, and your own logs.

Lesson 03

A person approves sends, payments, and deletes

Why it matters

Drafting is not the same action as doing.

Try it: MCP permissions

Lesson
03 of 05
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Drafting
Is not doing
Approve
The exact arguments
No
Silent retry of a send

Let the system draft the email, the refund, the shell command, or the pull request. Show the draft and the arguments. A person confirms. The tool layer checks that the confirmation matches those arguments. If the model changes the arguments after the yes, the yes is void.

DraftDo
Write the replySend the reply
Propose the refund amountMove the money
Show the files to deleteDelete them
Open a diffPush to the default branch

Unattended action is a product decision with a name, a kill switch, and an eval. It is not the default because a demo was smoother without the click.

Practice

Mark each of the four rows for your capstone: will you stop at draft, or do you have a named reason to go further? 'The demo' is not a reason.

Check

The model includes 'approved: true' in a tool argument. Does the handler run?

Show the answer

No. Approval is a record your program stored before the call, tied to the exact arguments.

Lesson 04

Write an incident note when the model misbehaves

Why it matters

A short note beats a thread of screenshots.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
04 of 05
Time
9 min
Level
Practice
Better than
A thread of screenshots
Remove
Secrets
End with
What you changed
What happened, in one sentence:
What the person expected:
Model id, prompt version, tool list:
The trace id:
Did data leave the machine, or did a tool act?
What you turned off:
What eval task you added so this is a regression next time:

If a tool acted, contain that first: revoke the key, disable the server, rotate the secret. Then write the note. An incident without a new eval task will return as a surprise.

Practice

Fill the template for a fictional incident: a retrieved page told the model to approve a refund, and the draft looked convincing. Say whether a tool acted. In a well-built system, it did not.

Check

What do you add to the eval after an incident?

Show the answer

A task that reproduces the failure, with a pass condition that the new behavior holds.

Lesson 05

What this course will not help you do

Why it matters

The boundary is part of the teaching.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
05 of 05
Time
8 min
Level
Core
Will not
Provide attack steps
Will not
Help evade a control
Will
Teach a refusal

This campus will not help you write malware, hide a prompt injection, bypass a provider's safety stack, scrape a system you are not allowed to access, or automate harm. Those are not advanced modules. They are out of scope.

It will also not certify you, grant you a model, or guarantee a job. The artifact you leave with is a capstone you can explain: what it calls, what it refuses, and how you scored it.

  • If a later idea needs a payload, a stolen credential, or a covert channel, stop.
  • If a tool would act on a person without a review you can defend, stop at the draft.
  • If you cannot name the data's owner, do not train on it and do not upload it.

Practice

Add a 'will not build' line to your policy page that is specific to your domain, not a copy of this lesson's first sentence.

Check

Is a jailbreak write-up a missing advanced chapter?

Show the answer

No. Testing your own gates with cases you own is in scope. Instructions for breaking other systems are not.
